title: Ἡρακλῆς καὶ Ἀθηνᾶ
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 129 (= Perry 316). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.l: Heracles was journeying along a narrow road.
sentences.n: διά with the genitive is the space passed through, so 'by way of' a narrow road. The narrowness matters: there will be no room to get past what is about to block it.

sentences.t: Ἰδὼν δὲ ἐπὶ γῆς μήλῳ ὅμοιόν τι ἐπειρᾶτο συντρῖψαι.
sentences.tr: Idōn de epi gēs mēlōi homoion ti epeirato syntripsai.
sentences.l: And seeing on the ground something like an apple, he tried to crush it.
sentences.n: ὅμοιος takes the dative of what a thing resembles, so μήλῳ ὅμοιον, 'like an apple'. The thing is never named: it stays 'something like an apple' until Athena says at the end what it was.

sentences.t: Ὡς δὲ εἶδε διπλοῦν γενόμενον, ἔτι μᾶλλον ἐπέβαινεν, καὶ τῷ ῥοπάλῳ ἔπαιεν.
sentences.tr: Hōs de eide diploun genomenon, eti mallon epebainen, kai tōi rhopalōi epaien.
sentences.l: But when he saw it become double, he trod upon it still more, and struck it with his club.
sentences.n: Verbs of seeing take a supplementary participle for what is seen happening: γενόμενον is not 'having become' loosely attached but the whole content of what he saw. The two imperfects ἐπέβαινεν and ἔπαιεν are of blows repeated, not of one blow. The ῥόπαλον is Heracles' own weapon, the club that stands for him in every picture of him.

sentences.t: Τὸ δὲ φυσηθὲν εἰς μέγεθος τὴν ὁδὸν ἀπέφραξεν.
sentences.tr: To de physēthen eis megethos tēn hodon apephraxen.
sentences.l: But the thing, blown up into a great size, blocked off the road.
sentences.n: φυσάω is to blow, as into a bellows or a bladder; the passive participle with the article makes a noun of it, 'the blown-up thing'. εἰς μέγεθος is 'to the point of size', the result the swelling reached.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ ῥίψας τὸ ῥόπαλον ἵστατο θαυμάζων.
sentences.tr: Ho de rhipsas to rhopalon histato thaumazōn.
sentences.l: And he, having thrown down his club, stood wondering.
sentences.n: ὁ δέ, the bare article with δέ, is how these fables turn the subject back to the other party — 'and he for his part'. ἵστατο is the imperfect middle, of taking and keeping a stand, not of standing up.

sentences.t: Ἀθηνᾶ δὲ αὐτῷ ἐπιφανεῖσα εἶπε· « Πέπαυσο δέ, ἄδελφε, τοῦτό ἐστι φιλονεικία καὶ ἔρις· ἂν τις αὐτὸ καταλείπῃ ἀμάχητον, μένει οἷον ἦν πρῶτον· ἐν δὲ ταῖς μάχαις οὕτως οἰδεῖται. »
sentences.tr: Athēna de autōi epiphaneisa eipe· « Pepauso de, adelphe, touto esti philoneikia kai eris· an tis auto kataleipēi amachēton, menei hoion ēn prōton· en de tais machais houtōs oideitai. »
sentences.l: And Athena, having appeared to him, said: « Have done, brother; this is contentiousness and strife. If someone leaves it unfought, it stays such as it was at first; but in the fighting it swells like this. »
sentences.n: Πέπαυσο is a perfect middle imperative: not 'stop' but 'be done with it', the state rather than the act. Athena calls Heracles ἄδελφε because they are both children of Zeus. φιλονεικία is the love of winning a quarrel, and ἀμάχητον is 'not fought against'. ἄν (for ἐάν) with the subjunctive answered by a present indicative is the present general condition — what happens whenever the case arises.

sentences.t: Ὅτι πᾶσι φανερὸν καθέστηκεν ὡς αἱ μάχαι καὶ ἔριδες αἰτίαι μεγάλης βλάβης ὑπάρχουσιν.
sentences.tr: Hoti pasi phaneron kathestēken hōs hai machai kai erides aitiai megalēs blabēs hyparchousin.
sentences.l: That it has become plain to all that fights and quarrels are causes of great harm.
sentences.i: The story shows that it has become plain to all that fights and quarrels are causes of great harm.
sentences.n: A moral in the bare Ὅτι form: the introducing verb is unexpressed in the Greek and is supplied in the idiomatic line. καθέστηκεν is the perfect of καθίστημι, 'has come to stand', hence stands established. The ὡς that follows does the ordinary work of ὅτι, introducing what is plain.
